title: The growing role of medical equipment rentals in making healthcare more accessible
summary: Vishal Lathwal, CEO, Apollo Homecare, explains how medical equipment rentals can reduce the financial burden of home-based recovery and improve access to post-discharge care
thbAction: Recommend THB's patient engagement workflows to improve acquisition, follow-up adherence, and post-discharge retention for expanding provider groups.
contentHtml:
When a patient is discharged from hospital, recovery does not end at the exit. For many people, especially those coming home after surgery, a stroke, a fracture or a respiratory illness, the weeks that follow are spent recovering at home, in familiar surroundings and with family close by.

But recovering safely at home often needs more than rest and medicines. Depending on the condition, a patient may need an adjustable hospital bed for safe positioning, a wheelchair to move around the house, or an oxygen concentrator if the doctor prescribes one. Families usually have to arrange this equipment within days of discharge, before the patient can be safely settled at home.

Each of these devices comes with its own price tag. Bought together, and on top of a hospital bill that has just been paid, they can add a heavy financial burden to an already expensive time. Most families in this situation ask the same question: do we have to buy all of this? The answer is no.

Paying for the weeks you need, not the years you don’t

The logic of medical equipment rental is straightforward enough that it is surprising it took this long to become widely accessible. A hospital bed needed for six weeks of post-operative recovery costs the same to purchase as one needed for ten years. Buying it means paying for permanent ownership of something that may be returned to a corner of the room once the recovery is complete.

Renting changes that calculation. The family pays for the period the equipment is actually in use and returns it when it is no longer required. For short recovery windows, renting could save a family roughly 50–70 per cent of the upfront cost of buying the same equipment. This is an illustrative range, not a guaranteed saving; actual savings will depend on the equipment, the rental duration and the service terms. 

The simplest way to look at it: why pay to own a device for years when you may only need it for a few weeks? Instead of paying the full purchase price on day one, families pay only for the weeks or months they actually use the equipment, and return it when the need ends. For a short recovery, that can make a meaningful difference to the household budget. A caregiver managing a parent’s post-stroke recovery at home already has enough to think about. Keeping a large part of the equipment budget free for medicines, physiotherapy or nursing support is one less thing to worry about.

When the list gets long

Recovery from a serious procedure rarely requires just one device. This is where the cost of buying versus renting becomes most visible.

A patient returning home after a respiratory event may need an oxygen concentrator for as long as the treating physician advises. At the same time, reduced mobility might require a hospital-grade adjustable bed for safe positioning, and a wheelchair for any movement around the home. Each of these has its own price. Purchased together, the family is facing a significant one-time expense that arrives simultaneously with ongoing medication costs, follow-up consultations, and the other financial pressures of managing a serious illness.

Renting all three devices for the recovery period, and returning them when the clinical need ends, spreads that cost very differently. For a short recovery, it could mean saving roughly 50–70 per cent of the upfront purchase expenditure, leaving that money free for the other costs of care. The exact mix of equipment should always follow the doctor’s advice; not every patient needs oxygen support or a full hospital-style setup at home.

Built for families in the middle

The families who benefit most from medical equipment rental are not necessarily those with the least resources. They are often families in the middle: managing a serious medical situation without an insurance policy that covers home equipment, or the savings to absorb a large one-time purchase without it affecting something else.

For them, being able to access hospital-grade equipment for the weeks or months it is clinically needed, pay only for that period, and return it when recovery is complete is not a small convenience. It can be the difference between managing care appropriately at home and being forced back into a clinical facility because the home cannot support the recovery.

One device, many patients

There is also a benefit that goes beyond the individual household. Purchased beds, wheelchairs and other devices often sit idle once recovery is complete, taking up space and proving difficult to resell. Rental equipment, by contrast, goes back into use: once returned, it is inspected, cleaned, serviced and supplied to the next patient who needs it. One well-maintained device can serve several families over its useful life instead of being bought separately by each one, keeping equipment in use and reducing avoidable purchases as demand for home-based care grows.

The market reflects the shift

It is little surprise, then, that more families are choosing to rent rather than buy. Apollo HomeCare’s own equipment rental business was reported to have nearly doubled year-on-year in FY26, with respiratory equipment forming a major share of demand. The wider market points in the same direction: India’s hospital-at-home equipment rental market is projected to grow at approximately 10.5 percent annually from 2026 to 2033, according to Grand View Research. That growth rate reflects a genuine shift in how families and healthcare providers are thinking about post-discharge care. The expectation that clinical care ends at the hospital exit is giving way to a more practical understanding: that recovery happens at home, over weeks and sometimes months, and that home needs to be equipped for it.

Alongside respiratory equipment, rental demand also spans mobility aids and hospital furniture. These are not niche products. They are the devices that determine whether a patient recovering at home can do so safely, comfortably, and with appropriate monitoring and support.

Accessible care starts with accessible equipment

The case for medical equipment rental ultimately goes beyond the individual family. For patients, it means paying for equipment only for as long as recovery needs it, and keeping more of the household budget for the rest of their care. For the wider healthcare system, it means the same devices are used far more efficiently: a shared rental fleet that is cleaned, serviced and redeployed serves many households, instead of separately purchased devices sitting idle once each recovery is complete.

It also supports a model of care that makes economic sense for providers. When patients can be equipped to recover safely at home, hospital beds stay available for those who need acute care, and providers can extend their services into the home without every family having to bear the full cost of ownership. As home-based recovery becomes a larger part of how healthcare is delivered in India, accessible equipment is not just a convenience for patients. It is part of what makes the system work more economically for everyone.
